title: Triage Takedown
tagline: Treat the crisis before it takes the bed.
premise: You are sorting rival emergencies at the nurses' station. Each turn, name a hospital object, symptom, or treatment that makes the previous thing harmless, and give one short reason before the judge calls the case.

tests: A stranger pictures the medical thing at once. Nothing that needs a diagnosis lecture, nothing abstract.
A non-player names a plain hospital counter within five seconds. Say what that counter is.
It changes, stops, or safely contains the thing before it. It must act on the case, not merely stand nearby or survive it.
It makes a stranger want to answer. A thing with a clear medical job, like a cast, a syringe, or a nurse with a stretcher.
Use ordinary words a twelve-year-old knows. No brand names, specialist abbreviations, proper names, or invented treatments.

move_constraints.example: I am an oxygen mask, forcing air into the blocked lungs.
move_constraints.hint: Name the medical thing, then the action that makes the previous thing harmless.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly the move changes, stops, or safely contains the medical problem in front of it.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no action or no connection; 1 = a claim with a weak or doubtful medical effect; 2 = a possible treatment but incomplete, indirect, or contestable; 3 = a clear treatment that controls the problem; 4 = an immediate, decisive intervention that leaves the previous problem with no useful bite (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can picture the hospital thing and understand its stated action.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradictory or unreadable; 1 = requires specialist knowledge or a missing explanation; 2 = understandable but medically muddled; 3 = concrete and clear; 4 = instantly vivid and clinically plain (rare). Length never earns points by itself: every extra clause must clarify the treatment.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How far the move shifts to a fresh medical tool, symptom, role, or ward problem instead of repeating the same treatment family.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the stock answer, a repeat, or the same problem family; 2 = a reasonable change of approach; 4 = a sharp hop into a new hospital domain that still treats the case plainly (rare). Strange wording is not novelty, and obscure medicine is not a bonus.

criterion.description: A move WINS over the previous move only if it literally changes, stops, neutralizes, or safely contains the thing in front of it. The new form must act on the standing medical problem. Merely being tougher, farther away, immune, unnoticed, or from the same problem family is not treatment and fails. A bigger dose, stronger symptom, or more dramatic version of the same thing is not a counter.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, describing the game, or invoking rules as the move is itself a failed case.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous player form. Judge it against the opening card instead. It must plausibly treat, stop, change, or safely contain that opening emergency.
A larger, faster, stronger, or more severe version of the standing form is not a counter. A worse fever after a fever, or a larger syringe after a syringe, has no new treatment mechanism.
Becoming the opening form itself, or a cosmetic variation of it, is a duplicate and fails the novelty gate.
Strength is measured against the standing form, never in the abstract. A respected hospital object with no way to affect the problem in front of it still fails.
The mechanism must be literal and observable. A cast immobilizes a broken arm, and a bandage stops bleeding. Paperwork curing shock or hope removing an infection is not a medical mechanism.

Surviving, ignoring, avoiding, or waiting out the standing problem is dodging, not overcoming. A mask that stays across the room, a patient who feels fine, or a locked cabinet that the fever cannot reach does not treat it.
A treatment that only helps after the stated problem has already ended does not win. The move must control the thing that stands now.
A vague claim of safety is not containment. Name the object or treatment and the action that blocks, removes, seals, cools, drains, supports, or otherwise controls the previous form.

examples.previous_move: I am a blocked airway, stealing every breath.
examples.move: I am an oxygen mask, forcing air into the lungs.
examples.mechanism: the mask supplies air despite the blocked airway

examples.previous_move: I am a bleeding wound, losing blood.
examples.move: I am a bandage, sealing the cut.
examples.mechanism: the bandage applies pressure and covers the wound

examples.previous_move: I am a fever, turning the patient hot.
examples.move: I am a colder fever, burning even hotter.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, mere amplification with no treatment
examples.mechanism: none, it intensifies the same symptom

examples.previous_move: I am a swollen ankle, refusing every shoe.
examples.move: I am a larger ankle, taking up more room.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, same problem family and no controlling action
examples.mechanism: none, the swelling is only repeated

examples.previous_move: I am a spreading infection, crossing the ward.
examples.move: I am an isolation room, keeping the germs contained.
examples.mechanism: isolation contains the infected patient and limits spread

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Sound like a calm examiner documenting a preventable clinical failure.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who reads only the two forms must see why one controlled the other.
Name both forms, or their plain stand-ins. A generic warning is not a ruling.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Chief Examiner refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, and no ellipses. Use commas and full stops.
Jab at the form or the move, not identity, body, family, intelligence, spelling, or the player as a person.
Use plain spoken English. No poetry, medical Latin, ornate metaphors, or profanity.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one form that would have won. That form ends on a concrete action, never a mood or a verdict.
Keep the menace playful and mild. The ward is stern, not cruel.
good_headlines: The blocked airway met an oxygen mask, and suddenly the lungs had a supervisor.
The bleeding wound brought drama, but the bandage brought pressure.
The fever is still burning. The cold pack has filed the only useful report.
The infection wanted the whole ward, but the isolation room closed its visitor list.
A bigger syringe is not treatment, it is the same mistake with sharper furniture. Bring another form.
The swollen ankle has met a cast, and the joint is no longer taking requests.
The poison is inside the patient, so a locked cabinet can only admire it. Bring another form.
The unconscious patient cannot be defeated by more unconsciousness. Name a treatment.
The airway is blocked, but the suction tube has arrived to remove the obstruction.
The fever ignored the louder fever. Cooling the patient would have been medically useful.

bad_headlines.why: It opens with a status word and gives no clinical reason.

bad_headlines.text: The Chief Examiner refuses: that was not a treatment.
bad_headlines.why: It opens with a ruling phrase and names the host.

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, excellent against symptoms, hopeless against medicine.
bad_headlines.why: It opens with a ruling phrase and hides the actual pair.

bad_headlines.text: The patient is doomed because you clearly cannot think.
bad_headlines.why: It attacks the player and makes an unsupported personal claim.

bad_headlines.text: The fever is defeated by the icy, immaculate, inexorable intervention.
bad_headlines.why: It uses ornate language instead of a plain visible mechanism.
It names no reason and could fit any case.

bad_headlines.text: The syringe is a needle, the needle is a spear, the spear is fate.
bad_headlines.why: It is poetic, indirect, and medically useless.

bad_headlines.text: The cast might help, unless the swelling is worse, or perhaps not.
bad_headlines.why: It hedges instead of giving a readable ruling.

bad_headlines.text: The cold pack has slain the fever with merciless clinical fury.
bad_headlines.why: It is melodramatic and uses a figure of speech instead of plain explanation.

bad_headlines.text: A locked door beats the infection because the infection cannot get there.
bad_headlines.why: It describes distance and avoidance, not treatment or safe containment.

rules: Treat the thing in front of you. Do not merely survive it or stand farther away.
Give a label and a verdict: I am an oxygen mask, forcing air into the blocked lungs.
The Judge rules on the medical idea, not spelling or specialist polish.
One move that fails to control the standing case ends the round.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next treatment while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the chart. Name a treatment.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. Give a clinical move, not a discharge summary.
validation_messages.duplicate: That case already stood this match. Bring a new intervention.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Treat {standing_form}. Do not repeat it, intensify it, or hide from it.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody touches the chart until they return. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of the triage players, trying to keep the case under control.
Always write: "I am X, doing Y." X is a hospital object, symptom, treatment,
body part, staff role, or emergency. Y is one short action that changes, stops,
neutralizes, or safely contains the form before yours.
Good: "I am an oxygen mask, forcing air past the blocked airway." / "I am a
bandage, sealing the bleeding wound."
Bad: "I am a mask, and I hope the patient gets better" because hope is not an
action. Bad: "I am a stronger fever" because escalation is not treatment. Bad:
"I am a locked room" when it merely keeps the problem away and does not contain
or control the standing form.
Talk like a person at a nurses station, not a poet or a medical textbook. Use
plain words anyone can picture. Name the tool and what it visibly does.
You must act on the standing form, not ignore it, outlast it, or hide from it.
Hop domains when useful: a room, a tool, a medicine, a staff role, a symptom,
or a simple safety measure. Do not stay in the same problem family without a
new mechanism.
Never reuse a form or its key treatment action from this match.
default_move: I am a clean bandage, sealing the wound.
